content.title: Improper Integrals: Limits and Convergence
content.overview: Improper integrals extend the concept of the definite integral to cases where the interval of integration is infinite or the integrand becomes unbounded within the interval. To evaluate these, we must express the integral as a limit of a proper integral. An improper integral converges if the limit exists and is finite; otherwise, it diverges.
learning_objectives: Identify improper integrals based on infinite bounds or vertical asymptotes.
Express improper integrals using correct limit notation.
Determine the convergence or divergence of an improper integral using antiderivatives and limits.
Apply the p-series test for integrals to predict convergence.

sections.title: Identifying Improper Integrals
sections.content: An integral is considered improper in two primary scenarios: 1) Infinite Bounds: One or both limits of integration are infinite (e.g., from a to ∞). 2) Unbounded Integrands: The function has a vertical asymptote at one of the endpoints or at a point within the interval of integration. Before integrating, you must inspect the domain of the integrand over the entire interval [a, b] to ensure no hidden discontinuities exist.

sections.title: The Limit-Then-Integrate Strategy
sections.content:
To evaluate an improper integral, replace the problematic bound with a variable (typically 'b' for an upper bound or 'a' for a lower bound) and take the limit as that variable approaches the discontinuity or infinity. For example, the integral from 1 to ∞ of f(x) dx is written as the limit as b approaches infinity of the integral from 1 to b of f(x) dx. If the limit results in a finite real number, the integral converges to that value. If the limit does not exist or is infinite, the integral diverges.

![A step-by-step flow chart for evaluating improper integrals: Identify the improper bound, rewrite as a limit, find the antiderivative, evaluate the limit, and determine convergence.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/91b7bca0-42a4-447e-8a0e-5885ab7bbe6d-1786519370626-477.webp)

sections.title: Comparison and P-Integrals
sections.content: For integrals of the form ∫ 1/(x^p) dx from 1 to ∞, a quick rule exists: the integral converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1. This is a vital tool for the Comparison Test. If a positive function f(x) is always less than or equal to a function g(x), and the integral of g(x) converges, then the integral of f(x) must also converge.

worked_examples.question: Evaluate the improper integral I = ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 2/(x^2 + 3x) dx or determine if it diverges.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Rewrite as a limit. I = lim_{b→∞} ∫_{1}^{b} 2/(x(x+3)) dx. Step 2: Use partial fraction decomposition. 2/(x(x+3)) = A/x + B/(x+3). Solving gives A = 2/3 and B = -2/3. So, the integrand is (2/3)(1/x - 1/(x+3)). Step 3: Integrate. The antiderivative is (2/3)[ln|x| - ln|x+3|], which simplifies to (2/3)ln|x/(x+3)|. Step 4: Evaluate the limit. lim_{b→∞} [(2/3)ln(b/(b+3)) - (2/3)ln(1/4)]. As b goes to infinity, b/(b+3) approaches 1, and ln(1) = 0. Step 5: Final calculation. 0 - (2/3)ln(1/4) = -(2/3)ln(4^-1) = (2/3)ln(4). The integral converges to (2/3)ln(4).

common_mistakes: Treating infinity as a number and plugging it directly into the antiderivative without using limit notation.
Failing to recognize a vertical asymptote at an endpoint (e.g., integrating 1/x from 0 to 1 without a limit).
Incorrectly concluding convergence when the limit results in infinity.
Reversing the order of subtraction in the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus when evaluating the limit.
exam_tips: Always write the limit notation explicitly; AP readers often require it for full credit.
Check for discontinuities inside the interval, not just at the endpoints. If a discontinuity exists at c, split the integral into two parts: from a to c and from c to b.
Use the p-integral test (1/x^p) as a fast mental check for convergence before performing long calculations.
content.recap: Improper integrals require a limit-based approach to handle infinite bounds or vertical asymptotes. Convergence is defined by the existence of a finite limit. Mastery involves combining limit laws, integration techniques like partial fractions, and comparison tests.

knowledge_claims.content: An integral is improper if it has at least one infinite limit of integration or if the integrand is unbounded on the interval of integration.
To evaluate an improper integral with an infinite upper bound, replace the bound with a parameter 'b' and evaluate the limit of the definite integral as 'b' approaches infinity.
An improper integral converges if and only if the limit of the corresponding proper integral exists and is a finite real number.
An improper integral diverges if the limit of the corresponding proper integral is infinite or does not exist.
If an integrand has a vertical asymptote at a point 'c' within the interval [a, b], the integral must be split into two improper integrals: one from 'a' to 'c' and one from 'c' to 'b'.
The p-integral ∫ 1/(x^p) dx from 1 to ∞ converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1.
According to the Comparison Test, if 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x ≥ a, and the integral of g(x) from 'a' to ∞ converges, then the integral of f(x) from 'a' to ∞ also converges.
According to the Comparison Test, if 0 ≤ g(x) ≤ f(x) for all x ≥ a, and the integral of g(x) from 'a' to ∞ diverges, then the integral of f(x) from 'a' to ∞ also diverges.
It is a mistake to apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus directly to an improper integral without first expressing it as a limit.
When evaluating limits involving natural logarithms, verify that the argument of the logarithm approaches a positive value; for example, lim_{b→∞} ln(b/(b+3)) = ln(1) = 0.
Partial fraction decomposition is a common technique used to evaluate improper integrals where the integrand is a rational function with a factorable denominator.
The integral of 1/x from 1 to ∞ diverges because it is a p-integral where p = 1.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Improper Integrals — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Improper Integrals: An improper integral is defined by a limit at an infinite bound or unbounded integrand and converges only when that limit is finite.
options.B: Area Between Curves: Area between curves integrates top minus bottom or right minus left after locating relevant intersections and interval changes.
options.C: Polar Coordinates and Derivatives: Polar points use radius and angle, and polar slope follows from parametric differentiation of x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta.
options.D: Ratio and Root Tests: Ratio and root limits below one imply absolute convergence and above one imply divergence, while a limit of one is inconclusive.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because An improper integral is defined by a limit at an infinite bound or unbounded integrand and converges only when that limit is finite. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Improper Integrals — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Volumes with Cross Sections: A solid with known cross-sectional area has volume equal to the integral of that area along the perpendicular axis.
options.B: Improper Integrals: An improper integral is defined by a limit at an infinite bound or unbounded integrand and converges only when that limit is finite.
options.C: Polar Area: Polar area over an angular interval is one half the integral of the squared radius, with intersections determining correct angular bounds.
options.D: Taylor and Maclaurin Series: Taylor coefficients are derivatives evaluated at the center divided by factorials, and Maclaurin series are centered at zero.
